title: Spherical solutions for stars
one_line_summary: Schutz's first strong-field chapter: symmetry arguments cut the metric of a static spherical spacetime down to two radial functions, Einstein's equations for a static perfect fluid become the mass-function and Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations, the vacuum exterior is Schwarzschild (unique by Birkhoff's theorem), two exact interiors (uniform density and Buchdahl) expose the compactness limit M/R < 4/9, and a long astrophysical survey explains degeneracy pressure, the Chandrasekhar limit, neutron stars, pulsars, supernovae and the compact-object mass gaps.
role_in_book: Chapters 1-9 built special relativity, tensors, curvature, the field equations and the weak-field regime (Newtonian limit and gravitational waves). Chapter 10 is the pivot to exact, strongly relativistic solutions. It is the first place the reader writes down a full metric ansatz, computes what the field equations demand, and integrates them with boundary and regularity conditions. It supplies the Schwarzschild metric that Chapter 11 reinterprets as a black hole (Buchdahl's theorem is the explicit bridge: stars more compact than 9M/4 must collapse), and its account of white dwarfs, neutron stars, pulsars and supernovae sets up the compact-binary sources of Chapter 12 and the Type Ia and nucleosynthesis remarks of Chapter 13.

assumed_background.topic: Metric components as dot products of coordinate basis vectors; line elements in general coordinates
Tensor component transformation under a coordinate change (Lambda matrices)
Perfect-fluid stress-energy tensor T = (rho + p) U U + p g and its components
First law of thermodynamics for a fluid element, dE = -p dV + Delta Q
Equation of state of radiation, p = rho/3
Computing Christoffel symbols, Riemann and Einstein tensors for a diagonal metric
Parallel transport on a two-sphere (why no nonvanishing symmetric vector field exists)
Conservation law T^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0 and Einstein's field equations G = 8 pi T
Conserved covariant momentum component p_0 when the metric is independent of t; observer-measured energy -p.U
Weak-field (Newtonian) metric of a distant mass M and its gravitational potential energy
Linearized-theory result that spherical pulsations radiate no gravitational waves; binary pulsars
Geometrized units G = c = 1 (solar mass about 1.47 km)
Spherical polar coordinates and the solid-angle element
Existence and uniqueness of solutions of first-order ordinary differential equations given initial values
Newtonian hydrostatic equilibrium of a self-gravitating ball of gas
Heisenberg uncertainty principle, spin-1/2 and the Pauli exclusion principle; counting states in phase space
Thermodynamics of a gas: pressure as -dE/dV at fixed entropy, specific entropy, sound speed
Basic stellar astrophysics: nuclear burning, main sequence, Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, supernovae

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why spherical symmetry lets one choose coordinates in which the metric takes the form of Eq. 10.5, and why the areal radius r is defined by the area of the symmetry spheres rather than by distance from a centre.
Reader can use the time-reversal transformation t -> -t to show that a static spherically symmetric metric has no dt dr cross term, and can distinguish static from stationary spacetimes.

Reader can read physical meaning off the metric functions: e^Lambda converts dr into proper radial distance, and e^Phi relates the conserved energy at infinity to locally measured energy and hence gives the redshift z = e^{-Phi} - 1.
Reader can write the stress-energy components of a static perfect fluid in these coordinates and derive the relativistic hydrostatic equation (rho + p) Phi' = -p'.
Reader can define the mass function m(r), derive dm/dr = 4 pi r^2 rho and the (r,r) equation for Phi', and explain why the (theta,theta) equation adds nothing new.

Reader can solve the vacuum equations to obtain the Schwarzschild metric, identify M with the Newtonian mass via the far-field limit, and state Birkhoff's theorem and its consequence that pulsating spherical stars emit no gravitational waves.

Reader can derive the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equation, set up a stellar model (regular centre m(0) = 0, central density as the single parameter, surface at p = 0, matching to Schwarzschild), and show that 2m(r) < r throughout a static star.
Reader can take the Newtonian limit of the TOV equation and explain how each relativistic correction steepens the required pressure gradient.
Reader can explain why M = integral of 4 pi r^2 rho dr is not the sum of proper energies of the fluid and where binding energy hides.

Reader can solve the uniform-density interior, obtain the central pressure as a function of M/R, and show that p_c diverges as M/R -> 4/9; reader can state Buchdahl's theorem and connect it to black-hole formation.
Reader can describe Buchdahl's exact solution, how its compactness parameter beta = M/R is limited by causality to beta < 1/6, and why it generalizes the n = 1 polytrope.
Reader can derive the equation of state of a cold degenerate Fermi gas by counting momentum cells, including the ultrarelativistic limit p = rho/3.
Reader can reproduce the order-of-magnitude Chandrasekhar mass argument for p = k rho^{4/3}, explaining why R cancels, and compare the estimate (about 0.3 solar masses) with the precise limit.

Reader can explain why neutron stars are many orders of magnitude denser than white dwarfs (about 10^17 versus at most 10^10 kg/m^3 in the book's figures), tracing this to the electron-neutron mass difference, estimate neutron-star radius, compactness and break-up spin, and summarize how pulsars were discovered and what mass measurements reveal.

Reader can outline the stellar-evolution pathways to white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes (roles of initial mass and metallicity) and the lower and upper mass gaps probed by gravitational-wave events.

teaching_approach.summary: The chapter proceeds from symmetry to solution to astrophysics. Coordinates are constructed by geometric requirements (spheres of known area, radial lines orthogonal to them, invariance under time reversal) rather than postulated, and each metric function is immediately given an operational meaning (proper distance, redshift). The Einstein tensor is quoted, not derived, so the effort goes into turning the field equations into a small ODE system with a physical reading (mass function, hydrostatic balance) and into careful boundary logic (regularity at the centre, p = 0 at the surface, matching to the exterior). Exact solutions serve as laboratories that reveal a general limit (4/9), which then becomes the doorway into gravitational collapse. The last third switches register to an order-of-magnitude, observation-rich narrative on degenerate matter, compact stars and supernovae, updated with 2019-2020 pulsar and gravitational-wave results.
narrative_arc: Motivate: most astrophysical bodies are nearly spherical, so spherical symmetry is the natural first strong-field problem.

Build coordinates from geometry: define r by the area of symmetry two-spheres, show with a throat surface that no centre is required, then use orthogonality to eliminate r-angle and t-angle cross terms (Eq. 10.5).
Specialize to static systems: define static via t-independence plus time-reversal invariance, kill g_0r, introduce Phi and Lambda and asymptotic flatness (Eqs. 10.7-10.8).
Interpret the metric: proper radial distance from e^Lambda, energy at infinity versus local energy, and the redshift formula z = e^{-Phi} - 1.

Quote the Einstein tensor for the static metric and the static perfect-fluid stress-energy; add an equation of state and the single nontrivial conservation equation (relativistic hydrostatic balance).
Introduce the mass function to make the (0,0) equation look Newtonian; obtain the (r,r) equation; note the angular equation is redundant by the Bianchi identity.
Solve in vacuum to obtain Schwarzschild; check against the weak-field metric to identify M; invoke Birkhoff's theorem for generality and the absence of monopole gravitational radiation.

Inside the star: derive TOV, state the integration recipe (m(0) = 0 from local flatness, central density as parameter, surface at p = 0, continuity with the exterior), and warn that M is not the sum of proper energies.
Prove that 2m < r in any static star and take the Newtonian limit, showing GR steepens the pressure gradient (foreshadowing collapse).
Test the machinery on exact solutions: uniform density (p_c -> infinity at M/R = 4/9) and Buchdahl's causal solution (beta < 1/6, redshift up to 0.22).
Generalize to Buchdahl's theorem and argue that an over-compact star must collapse, leaving a Schwarzschild exterior: the black hole of Chapter 11.
Switch to astrophysics: stellar evolution to giants, the gravothermal instability, and the branching fates set by initial mass.
Model the supporting physics: count Fermi states to get degeneracy pressure, then estimate the Chandrasekhar mass by dimensional reasoning.
Neutron stars: neutronization instability, compactness and spin estimates, pulsar discovery and mass measurements, equation-of-state uncertainty, kicks.
Close with supernova fates, metallicity, the lower and upper mass gaps and the gravitational-wave events that probe them, pointing forward to Chapters 11-13.
signature_moves: Coordinates defined by invariant geometric properties (area of the symmetry spheres) with an explicit warning that the label r carries no a priori distance meaning.
Symmetry arguments done with transformation matrices: the t -> -t Lambda matrix flips the sign of g_0r, so staticity forces it to vanish.
Every metric function earns an operational meaning at once (proper distance for g_rr, redshift and energy at infinity for g_00) before the field equations are touched.

Change of unknown from Lambda to m(r) chosen so the field equation mirrors Newtonian mass accounting, immediately followed by a caution about non-localizable energy and coordinate versus proper volume.
Physics-style proofs by contradiction and local-flatness arguments (m(0) = 0 from circumference/radius; 2m < r because pressure would crash to zero first).
Exact solutions used as probes that reveal a general theorem (4/9 limit) instead of as ends in themselves.
Order-of-magnitude replacements of differential equations by algebraic scalings (d/dr -> 1/R) to extract the Chandrasekhar mass, with the observation that R cancels.
Vivid comparison numbers for scale (a city-sized star, a star spinning twenty times faster than a car engine).
Contemporary observational anchors (PSR J0740+6620, GW190814, GW190521, Philippov et al. 2019) woven into a textbook derivation chapter.

sections.title: Coordinates for spherically symmetric spacetimes
sections.summary: Starts from flat space in spherical coordinates, notes that the coefficient of dOmega^2 fixes both the area and circumference of a sphere, and uses this to define spherical symmetry in a curved spacetime: every event lies on a two-sphere, and r is defined so that the sphere's area is 4 pi r^2. A throat surface (Figure 10.1) shows that circles need not surround any point of the space, so symmetry does not imply a centre. Requiring radial coordinate lines and time lines to meet the spheres orthogonally removes all cross terms between the angles and (t, r), leaving three unknown functions of (t, r).
key_moves: Read circumference 2 pi sqrt(coefficient) and area 4 pi (coefficient) off the two-sphere line element; conversely any surface with that line element is a sphere.
Define r through f(r', t) := r^2, a coordinate transformation that makes r an area label with no guaranteed link to proper distance from a centre.
Figure 10.1 counterexample: an axially symmetric two-space whose circles have no centre within the space.
Align the angular coordinates of neighbouring spheres by making theta, phi = const lines orthogonal to the spheres: g_r theta = g_r phi = 0 (Eq. 10.4).
Full spacetime symmetry (no preferred direction on the spheres) forces g_t theta = g_t phi = 0, giving Eq. 10.5.

sections.title: Static spherically symmetric spacetimes
sections.summary: Defines a static spacetime by two conditions (metric independent of t and invariant under t -> -t), contrasting it with a stationary rotating star. The time-reversal transformation flips the sign of g_0r, so it must vanish, giving the diagonal metric with e^{2 Phi} and e^{2 Lambda}; asymptotic flatness sets Phi, Lambda -> 0. The section interprets the metric: e^Lambda gives proper radial distance, the conserved E = -p_0 is energy at infinity while a static local observer measures e^{-Phi} E, and a photon climbing out from r_1 has redshift e^{-Phi(r_1)} - 1. It ends by quoting the nonzero Einstein tensor components for this metric.
concepts: gravitational redshift in a static spacetime
Einstein tensor of the static spherical metric
key_moves: Static = (i) t-independent components plus (ii) invariance under t -> -t; rotating stars satisfy (i) only (stationary).
Apply Lambda^0_0 = -1: g_00 and g_rr unchanged, g_0r changes sign, hence g_0r = 0 (Eq. 10.6).
Replace g_00, g_rr by -e^{2 Phi}, e^{2 Lambda}, valid only while g_00 < 0 and g_rr > 0; flag that black holes violate this.
Static observer has U^0 = e^{-Phi}; E* = -U.p = e^{-Phi} E, so E is the energy measured at infinity.
Photon emitted with local frequency nu_em arrives with nu_em e^{Phi(r_1)}: z = e^{-Phi(r_1)} - 1 (Eq. 10.13).
Einstein tensor components Eqs. 10.14-10.17 stated without derivation (derivation deferred to Exercise 10.4).

sections.title: Static perfect-fluid Einstein equations
sections.summary: For a fluid at rest the only velocity component is U^0 = e^{-Phi}, giving diagonal stress-energy components. An equation of state p(rho, S), reduced to p(rho) when entropy is constant, closes the system. Of the four conservation equations only the radial one survives, relating the pressure gradient to Phi'. Replacing Lambda with the mass function m(r) turns the (0,0) Einstein equation into dm/dr = 4 pi r^2 rho, formally Newtonian though m is not localizable mass-energy; the (r,r) equation gives Phi' in terms of m and p. The angular equations are redundant by the Bianchi identities, leaving four equations for Phi, m, rho, p.
concepts: Bianchi identity redundancy of field equations
key_moves: Normalization U.U = -1 with only U^0 nonzero gives U^0 = e^{-Phi}, U_0 = -e^{Phi}.
T_00 = rho e^{2 Phi}, T_rr = p e^{2 Lambda}, T_theta theta = r^2 p from the perfect-fluid tensor.
Symmetry leaves only the alpha = r conservation equation: (rho + p) Phi' = -p'.
Define m(r) = r(1 - e^{-2 Lambda})/2 so g_rr = (1 - 2m/r)^{-1}; the (0,0) equation becomes dm/dr = 4 pi r^2 rho.
The (r,r) equation yields Phi' = (m + 4 pi r^3 p)/[r(r - 2m)].
Count equations and unknowns; the (theta,theta) equation follows from the others via the Bianchi identity.

sections.title: The exterior geometry
sections.summary: Outside the star rho = p = 0, so m is a constant M and Phi' = M/[r(r - 2M)], which integrates (with Phi -> 0 at infinity) to e^{2 Phi} = 1 - 2M/r: the Schwarzschild metric. Expanding for large r and transforming to quasi-Cartesian (isotropic) coordinates reproduces the weak-field metric of a mass M, justifying the name. Birkhoff's theorem, cited from Misner, Thorne and Wheeler, extends uniqueness to non-static spherical spacetimes, so even a pulsating or collapsing spherical star has a static exterior and radiates no gravitational waves, just as there is no electromagnetic monopole radiation.
key_moves: Vacuum equations dm/dr = 0 and Phi' = m/[r(r - 2m)] integrate to m = M and e^{2 Phi} = 1 - 2M/r.
Large-r expansion (Eq. 10.37) plus a coordinate change (Exercise 10.9) matches the Newtonian far-field metric (Eq. 8.60), so M is the mass seen by distant orbits.
Birkhoff: the result holds without assuming staticity, starting from Eq. 10.5.
Consequence: spherical pulsation or collapse cannot change the exterior and cannot radiate, echoing the linearized result of Exercise 9.47.

sections.title: The interior structure of the star
sections.summary: Eliminating Phi between the hydrostatic and (r,r) equations gives the TOV equation. Together with dm/dr and an equation of state it forms a closed system whose integration needs m(0) = 0 (forced by local flatness at the centre) and a central pressure or density, so for a fixed equation of state stellar models form a one-parameter family. The surface is where p reaches zero; matching g_rr to Schwarzschild fixes M = m(R), and matching g_00 supplies the boundary value for Phi. M equals the integral of 4 pi r^2 rho dr, but that is not proper volume, so binding energy is hidden in the difference. The section notes the first real use of a regular centre, proves 2m(r) < r everywhere in a static star, and recovers Newtonian hydrostatic equilibrium in the weak limit, observing that all relativistic terms steepen the pressure gradient.
concepts: gravitational binding energy in the total mass
compactness bound 2m < r in static stars
Newtonian limit of the TOV equation
pressure as a source of gravity
key_moves: Divide Eq. 10.27 by rho + p and substitute into Eq. 10.31 to obtain TOV (Eq. 10.39); Phi becomes subsidiary.
Local flatness at r = 0: circumference/proper radius must be 2 pi, so g_rr(0) = 1 and m/r -> 0.
Two first-order ODEs need two initial data; with m(0) = 0 fixed, the central density labels the model (ODE uniqueness).
Continuity of p (finite forces) puts the surface at p = 0; continuity of g_rr gives M = m(R); continuity of g_00 fixes Phi inside.
Proper volume element e^Lambda r^2 sin theta dr dtheta dphi differs from 4 pi r^2 dr, so M is not a sum of proper energies.
If r - 2m approached zero the TOV gradient would scale like -1/epsilon and drive p to zero first, so 2m < r always.
Newtonian limit p << rho, m << r gives dp/dr = -rho m/r^2; each correction factor (rho+p, m+4 pi r^3 p, r-2m) makes the gradient steeper.

sections.title: Exact interior solutions: the uniform-density (Schwarzschild interior) star
sections.summary: Exact solutions are rare, and those built by guessing m(r) usually imply unphysical equations of state (footnote 1). Assuming constant density, although it implies an infinite sound speed, makes TOV integrable: m grows as r^3, the pressure satisfies a closed algebraic relation with the central pressure, and the radius, central pressure, pressure profile and e^Phi follow in closed form. The central pressure diverges as M/R approaches 4/9, a limit later shown to be general. Phi and m increase outward while p decreases.
concepts: speed of sound and causality in stellar matter
key_moves: rho = const replaces the equation of state; m = 4 pi rho r^3/3 inside and M outside by continuity of g_rr.
TOV becomes separable (Eq. 10.48) and integrates to Eq. 10.49 with 1 - 2m/r = 1 - 2Mr^2/R^3.
Setting p(R) = 0 gives R in terms of p_c (10.50) or p_c in terms of M/R (10.51); substituting gives the profile (10.52).
p_c -> infinity when 3 sqrt(1 - 2M/R) = 1, i.e. M/R = 4/9.
Phi from Eq. 10.27 with the boundary value g_00(R) = -(1 - 2M/R) (Eq. 10.54).

sections.title: Exact interior solutions: Buchdahl's interior solution
sections.summary: Buchdahl's 1981 solution uses the equation of state rho = 12 sqrt(p_* p) - 5p, which reduces to an n = 1 polytrope at low pressure and can be kept causal. It is written in an auxiliary radial coordinate r' with u = beta sin(Ar')/(Ar'); the metric functions, pressure and density are given explicitly, the surface sits at Ar' = pi, and beta turns out to equal M/R there, fixing the surface redshift. The constant p_* only sets the length scale; beta controls how relativistic the model is. Requiring the sound speed below light at the centre limits beta < 1/6, spanning Newtonian stars to surface redshift 0.22.
concepts: speed of sound and causality in stellar matter
key_moves: Causality dp/drho < 1 applied to the equation of state gives p < p_*, rho < 7 p_* (10.57).
Auxiliary coordinate r' defined implicitly through u(r') (Eqs. 10.58-10.59); solution quoted, verification left to Exercise 10.12.
At the surface u = 0: e^{2 Phi} = e^{-2 Lambda} = 1 - 2 beta, so beta = M/R and z_s = (1 - 2 beta)^{-1/2} - 1.
Scaling argument: p_* fixes units only; beta is the physical parameter.
p/rho is largest at the centre, beta/(2 - 5 beta); demanding it be below 1/7 gives 0 < beta < 1/6.

sections.title: Realistic stars and gravitational collapse: Buchdahl's theorem and stellar evolution
sections.summary: Buchdahl's 1959 theorem generalizes the 4/9 bound to any static star: no equilibrium exists with R < 9M/4, so a star pushed inward from that configuration must collapse, and Birkhoff guarantees its exterior stays Schwarzschild, leaving a black hole. The section then sketches stellar evolution: hydrogen burning on the main sequence, the negative specific heat of self-gravitating systems, helium ignition and red giants with strong winds, white dwarfs for initial masses below about 8 solar masses, and for heavier stars burning through to iron followed by core collapse to a proto-neutron star, with three possible outcomes as the envelope falls back.
concepts: negative specific heat of self-gravitating systems
key_moves: Promote the uniform-density 4/9 result to a theorem valid for any equation of state.
Thought experiment: an inward push on a 9M/4 star cannot end in a new equilibrium; exterior stays Schwarzschild.
Negative specific heat: losing energy makes a star's core hotter, the engine of the gravito-thermal instability.
Mass loss during the giant phase decides the branch: below about 8 solar masses a C/O white dwarf; above, burning to iron and core collapse.
Iron-56 as the most bound nucleus ends thermal support; core falls from Earth size to about 10 km and neutronizes.

sections.title: Realistic stars and gravitational collapse: quantum-mechanical pressure
sections.summary: An elementary derivation of degeneracy pressure. The uncertainty principle assigns each state a momentum-space cell of size h^3/V; with two spin states per cell and Pauli exclusion, the coldest configuration of N fermions fills a Fermi sphere up to p_f, which depends only on number density. Integrating the energy gives rho, and p = -dE/dV at fixed N gives the pressure. In the ultrarelativistic limit rho is proportional to p_f^4 and p = rho/3, the photon-gas law, because rest mass becomes irrelevant.
concepts: Pauli exclusion principle and phase-space cells
ultrarelativistic equation of state p = rho/3
key_moves: Cell counting: dN = V 4 pi p^2 dp/h^3 states, doubled for spin.
Cold gas fills states up to p_f: n = 8 pi p_f^3/(3 h^3), independent of particle mass.
Energy density as integral of sqrt(m^2 + p^2) over the Fermi sphere; pressure from the first law with Delta Q = 0.
Use p_f proportional to V^{-1/3} to evaluate dE/dV, yielding Eq. 10.77.
For p_f >> m: rho ~ 2 pi p_f^4/h^3 and p ~ rho/3.

sections.title: Realistic stars and gravitational collapse: white dwarfs
sections.summary: In a compressed star electrons and nuclei form separate gases at the same temperature; electrons, being light, reach degeneracy first and supply the pressure, while nuclei supply almost all the mass. With rho = mu m_p n_e the relativistic electron gas gives p = k rho^{4/3}. Replacing the Newtonian structure equations by order-of-magnitude scalings, the radius cancels and a unique mass emerges, about 0.32 solar masses for mu = 2; careful integration gives the Chandrasekhar limit near 1.3 solar masses, slightly lowered by the neutronization instability at about 10^10 kg/m^3. White dwarfs may be half the Galaxy's stars but are faint.
key_moves: Separate roles: electron gas provides pressure, nuclear gas provides gravitating mass (rho = mu m_p n_e).
Combine ultrarelativistic electron EOS with n_e = rho/(mu m_p) to get p = k rho^{4/3} with k built from h, mu, m_p.
Scale dm/dr and dp/dr as M ~ R^3 rho-bar and p-bar/R ~ rho-bar M/R^2.
Substituting the 4/3 law makes R drop out, so the balance fixes M itself: a limiting mass.
Numerical estimate 0.47 x 10^5 cm = 0.32 solar masses versus the precise 1.3 solar masses.

sections.title: Realistic stars and gravitational collapse: neutron stars and pulsars
sections.summary: Above white-dwarf densities electrons combine with protons, removing pressure and triggering collapse until neutron degeneracy halts it near 10^17 kg/m^3. Neutron stars differ from white dwarfs in needing far higher density to make neutrons relativistic and in having no separate mass-carrying gas, so p = rho/3 applies and only the full relativistic equations can yield a maximum mass. Estimates: radius about 17 km from the mean density (observed 10-12 km), M/R about 0.15, break-up spin about 1.8 kHz, and large binding-energy release. History (Baade and Zwicky 1934; Bell and Hewish 1967), pulsar phenomenology and emission models, exotic interior physics, equation-of-state uncertainty, measured masses clustering near 1.4 solar masses with PSR J0740+6620 at 2.14, GW constraints including GW190814, spin-up by accretion, rotational support and natal kicks are surveyed.
concepts: gravitational binding energy release in collapse
neutron-star equation of state and maximum mass
key_moves: Inverse beta decay removes electrons under compression, so pressure lags density: an instability gap between white dwarfs and neutron stars.
Neutron gas is both pressure and mass source, so the EOS is p = rho/3 with no dimensional constant; no simple mass-limit argument.
Mean density 10^17 kg/m^3 and 1 solar mass give R about 17 km; realistic 10-12 km gives M/R ~ 0.15, about three times the Buchdahl minimum radius.
Break-up speed sqrt(M/R) = 0.39 gives period 0.54 ms (1.8 kHz), versus 716 Hz for the fastest known pulsar.
Energy of a particle at rest on the surface as seen from infinity implies a large fraction of rest mass released (see gaps for a misprint).
Supernova mass loss usually unbinds binaries; a suitable kick can keep them bound, so double neutron stars are rare.

sections.title: Realistic stars and gravitational collapse: supernovae and compact-object mass gaps
sections.summary: The fate of a collapsing core depends on mass, rotation, magnetic field and composition. Roughly 8-25 solar-mass stars leave neutron stars via neutrino-driven Type II supernovae that also forge elements up to iron; heavier, low-metallicity stars suffer fallback onto the core and form black holes of about 5-60 solar masses, with hypernovae and long gamma-ray bursts for the most massive. The upper limit of neutron-star masses and the lower limit of supernova black holes define a lower mass gap (partly filled by neutron-star mergers, e.g. GW190814); an instability that disrupts very massive stars and the possible remnants of zero-metallicity first stars define an upper gap around 60-150 solar masses (GW190521). Rotation, magnetic fields and binary interaction complicate the picture.
key_moves: Map initial mass ranges to remnants: 8-25 solar masses to neutron stars; above 25 depends on metallicity.
Opacity of heavy elements controls how much envelope is expelled and how massive stars can form.
Lower mass gap between about 2.5-3 and 5 solar masses; upper gap 60-150 solar masses from a disruptive instability.
Gravitational-wave events already place objects inside both gaps.

Flags that continuity of g_00 and g_rr is a simplification of the full junction conditions.

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Nineteen problems: coordinate transformations to spherical and isotropic forms, symmetry proofs (why cross terms and non-radial conservation equations vanish), deriving every structure equation, completing the uniform-density and Buchdahl solutions with numbers for the Sun and a neutron star, the n = 1 polytrope as the Newtonian limit of Buchdahl, a series expansion near the centre for numerical work, a scaling argument for p = rho/3 stars, a numerical stiff neutron-star sequence, and estimates of collapse-induced spin-up and magnetic-field amplification.
concepts: ultrarelativistic equation of state p = rho/3
key_moves: Exercise 10.9 builds isotropic coordinates and proves the far-field form Eq. 10.38.
Exercises 10.15 and 10.17 turn the chapter into a numerical stellar-structure project.

concepts.name: spherically symmetric spacetime
concepts.definition: A spacetime in which every event lies on a two-dimensional surface with the intrinsic geometry of a round sphere, and the geometry is invariant under the rotations of those spheres, so no direction tangent to them is preferred.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the near-sphericity of stars; made precise by generalizing the flat-space fact that surfaces of constant t and r are two-spheres with line element r^2 dOmega^2.

concepts.name: two-sphere line element
concepts.definition: The intrinsic metric r^2(dtheta^2 + sin^2 theta dphi^2) of a sphere; the coefficient of dOmega^2 determines the sphere's area (4 pi times it) and circumference (2 pi times its square root), and any surface with this form of line element is intrinsically a sphere.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from Minkowski space in spherical coordinates at fixed t and r (Eqs. 10.1-10.2).

concepts.name: areal radius
concepts.definition: The radial coordinate r defined so that the symmetry two-sphere through an event has proper area 4 pi r^2 (circumference 2 pi r); it is not in general the proper distance from any centre, which is instead the integral of sqrt(g_rr) dr.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by a coordinate transformation f(r',t) := r^2 on the unknown sphere-area function; the text stresses that r is determined by the spheres alone and has no a priori link to radial distance.
concepts.notes: Learners routinely read r as distance from the centre; the chapter's proper-distance formula (10.9) is the corrective.

concepts.name: spherical symmetry without a centre
concepts.definition: Spherical (or axial) symmetry constrains only the geometry of the symmetry orbits; it does not require the space to contain a point at their common centre, since that centre is not a point on the spheres themselves.
concepts.how_introduced: Illustrated with Figure 10.1: two flat sheets joined by a throat have circles of every circumference about an axis, but the axis is not part of the surface. Revisited when building interior solutions, which are the first place a regular centre r = 0 is assumed.
concepts.notes: Foreshadows the black-hole and wormhole geometries of Chapter 11, where r = 0 behaves very differently.

concepts.name: adapted coordinates for spherical symmetry
concepts.definition: Choosing coordinates so that the lines of constant angles are orthogonal to the symmetry spheres (g_r theta = g_r phi = 0) and so that time lines are also orthogonal to them (g_t theta = g_t phi = 0), which aligns the angular coordinates of neighbouring spheres and removes any preferred tangential direction.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by noting that nothing yet relates the pole orientation of the sphere at r to that at r + dr; orthogonality is imposed as the natural choice, then justified for e_t by the no-preferred-direction argument (elaborated in Exercise 10.2).
prerequisites: metric components as basis dot products

concepts.name: general spherically symmetric metric
concepts.definition: The most general metric of a spherically symmetric spacetime in adapted coordinates: ds^2 = g_00 dt^2 + 2 g_0r dr dt + g_rr dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2, with the three functions depending on t and r.
concepts.how_introduced: End point of the orthogonality arguments of §10.1; later the starting point for Birkhoff's theorem.

concepts.name: static spacetime
concepts.definition: A spacetime admitting a time coordinate t such that all metric components are independent of t and the geometry is unchanged under t -> -t; equivalently, a time-independent geometry with no rotation-like cross terms between time and space.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as the simplest situation for a quiet star or black hole, with the image of a film that looks the same run backwards; distinguished from stationary with the rotating-star example.
concepts.notes: The book's definition is coordinate-based; the invariant version uses a hypersurface-orthogonal timelike Killing vector, not mentioned here.

concepts.name: stationary spacetime
concepts.definition: A spacetime with a time coordinate in which the metric components do not depend on time, without the additional requirement of time-reversal invariance; a uniformly rotating star is stationary but not static.
concepts.how_introduced: Given in parentheses as the weaker of the two conditions in the static definition.

concepts.name: time-reversal argument for staticity
concepts.definition: Applying the coordinate change t -> -t (Lambda^0_0 = -1) to the metric leaves g_00 and g_rr unchanged but reverses the sign of g_0r; if the geometry must be invariant, g_0r must vanish.
concepts.how_introduced: Worked in Eq. 10.6 using the tensor transformation law; Exercise 10.5 reuses it to show a static fluid has no spatial velocity.

concepts.name: metric functions Phi and Lambda
concepts.definition: Radial functions defined by g_00 = -e^{2 Phi} and g_rr = e^{2 Lambda} in the static spherical metric; the exponential form presumes g_00 < 0 and g_rr > 0. Phi plays the role of a relativistic gravitational potential (it controls redshift) and e^Lambda converts dr to proper distance.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as replacement unknowns in Eq. 10.7, with the warning that the sign conditions fail for black holes and will force a new look at coordinates in Chapter 11.

concepts.name: asymptotic flatness
concepts.definition: The requirement that far from an isolated source the spacetime approaches Minkowski space; for the static spherical metric it means Phi and Lambda tend to zero as r -> infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Imposed as the boundary condition appropriate to bounded systems like stars (Eq. 10.8); used to fix the integration constant in the exterior solution.

concepts.name: proper radial distance
concepts.definition: The physical length of a purely radial curve at fixed t, theta, phi between two radii, obtained by integrating sqrt(g_rr) dr = e^Lambda dr; it generally differs from the difference of areal radii.
concepts.how_introduced: First physical interpretation of a metric component (Eq. 10.9); reused in the central-regularity argument.

concepts.name: energy at infinity
concepts.definition: For a geodesic in a time-independent metric the covariant component p_0 is conserved; E := -p_0 is the energy the particle would be measured to have by a static observer far away where e^Phi = 1.
concepts.how_introduced: Uses the Chapter 7 result that p_0 is constant when the metric does not depend on t, then contrasts E with what a local static observer measures.

concepts.name: locally measured energy
aliases: energy relative to a static observer
concepts.definition: The energy E* = -U.p of a particle measured by an observer momentarily at rest at radius r; with U^0 = e^{-Phi} this is e^{-Phi} E, larger than the energy at infinity where e^{-Phi} > 1, the excess being kinetic energy gained by falling.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the static observer's four-velocity; Exercise 10.3 shows the weak-field difference E* - E is the Newtonian potential energy.

concepts.name: gravitational redshift in a static spacetime
concepts.definition: A photon emitted with frequency nu_em by a static source at r_1 has conserved E = h nu_em e^{Phi(r_1)}, so a distant observer receives nu_rec = nu_em e^{Phi(r_1)} and measures redshift z = e^{-Phi(r_1)} - 1; this gives e^Phi a direct observational meaning.
concepts.how_introduced: Applied to photons as the most significant case of the energy-at-infinity argument; compared to an earlier chapter's redshift calculation. Reused for the Buchdahl surface redshift and Exercise 10.10.

concepts.name: Einstein tensor of the static spherical metric
concepts.definition: The nonvanishing components G_00, G_rr, G_theta theta and G_phi phi = sin^2 theta G_theta theta computed from ds^2 = -e^{2Phi} dt^2 + e^{2Lambda} dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2, expressed through Phi, Lambda and their r-derivatives.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated without derivation ('one can show'); the computation is Exercise 10.4 via Exercise 6.35, and the bibliography recommends computer algebra or Cartan's method.

concepts.name: four-velocity of a static fluid
concepts.definition: For fluid at rest in static coordinates only U^0 is nonzero, and normalization U.U = -1 fixes U^0 = e^{-Phi}, U_0 = -e^{Phi}.
concepts.how_introduced: Deduced from the static assumption and normalization (Exercise 10.5 justifies that spatial components vanish).

concepts.name: perfect fluid stress-energy tensor
concepts.definition: T^{alpha beta} = (rho + p) U^alpha U^beta + p g^{alpha beta}, with rho the total energy density and p the isotropic pressure in the fluid rest frame; for a static fluid in the static spherical metric its nonzero covariant components are rho e^{2Phi}, p e^{2Lambda}, r^2 p and r^2 sin^2 theta p.
concepts.how_introduced: Imported from Chapter 4 (Eqs. 4.37-4.38) and evaluated in the new coordinates.

concepts.name: equation of state
concepts.definition: A relation specifying the pressure of a fluid in local thermodynamic equilibrium in terms of its energy density and specific entropy, p = p(rho, S); when entropy is uniform or negligible it reduces to a one-variable relation p = p(rho) that closes the stellar-structure equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the missing link between rho and p in T; later instantiated by uniform density, Buchdahl's law, the degenerate-gas laws p = k rho^{4/3} and p = rho/3, and a piecewise stiff law in Exercise 10.17.
concepts.notes: Exercise 10.7: a general p(rho, S) requires an extra free function such as S(r).

concepts.name: relativistic hydrostatic equilibrium
aliases: relativistic Euler equation for a static fluid
concepts.definition: The only nontrivial component of T^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0 for a static spherical fluid: (rho + p) dPhi/dr = -dp/dr, stating that the pressure gradient must balance gravity, with inertia measured by rho + p rather than rho.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from the conservation law with the remark that symmetry kills the t, theta, phi components (Exercise 10.8 asks for a short symmetry proof).

concepts.name: mass function
concepts.definition: The function m(r) defined by g_rr = (1 - 2m(r)/r)^{-1}, i.e. m = r(1 - e^{-2Lambda})/2; the (0,0) Einstein equation gives dm/dr = 4 pi r^2 rho, and its value at the surface is the mass measured by distant orbits, but it is not the localized mass-energy inside r.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a change of unknown chosen so that the (0,0) equation takes the Newtonian form; immediately qualified by the non-localizability of gravitational energy and later by the coordinate-versus-proper-volume discussion.
prerequisites: Einstein tensor of the static spherical metric

concepts.name: non-localizability of gravitational energy
concepts.definition: In general relativity there is no well-defined energy density of the gravitational field, so total energy (including gravitational binding) cannot be assigned to particular regions; only global quantities such as the mass seen from infinity are unambiguous.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked in one sentence to explain why m(r) should not be called the mass-energy inside r; illustrated concretely by the gap between coordinate and proper volume in §10.5.
concepts.notes: Backward pointer to the Chapter 7 caution about energy in GR.

concepts.name: Bianchi identity redundancy of field equations
concepts.definition: Because the Einstein tensor is identically divergence-free, once the conservation equations and some components of Einstein's equations hold, the remaining components are automatically satisfied; for the static star the (theta,theta) equation follows from the (0,0), (r,r) and hydrostatic equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to justify ignoring the angular equation when counting four equations for four unknowns.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild metric
concepts.definition: The vacuum, static, spherically symmetric, asymptotically flat solution ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r) dt^2 + (1 - 2M/r)^{-1} dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2, describing the exterior of any spherical body of mass M.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by setting rho = p = 0 in the structure equations and integrating with Phi -> 0 at infinity; checked against the weak-field metric.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild mass
concepts.definition: The constant M in the exterior metric, equal to m(R) at the stellar surface; identified with the Newtonian mass because the far-field metric matches the weak-field metric of a mass M, so it is what Kepler's law for distant orbits measures.
concepts.how_introduced: Justified by expanding Schwarzschild at large r and passing to quasi-Cartesian coordinates (Eq. 10.38 versus Eq. 8.60), then fixed from the interior by continuity of g_rr (Eq. 10.40).

concepts.name: isotropic coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates in which the spatial part of a spherically symmetric metric is conformally flat, proportional to dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2; for Schwarzschild they follow from r = r-bar(1 + M/2r-bar)^2 and make the weak-field form manifest.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted to exist in the text (Eq. 10.38) and constructed in Exercise 10.9, which also notes the horizon r = 2M maps to r-bar = M/2.
formulas: ds^2=-\left(\frac{1-M/2\bar r}{1+M/2\bar r}\right)^2dt^2+\left(1+\frac{M}{2\bar r}\right)^4(d\bar r^2+\bar r^2d\Omega^2)

concepts.name: Birkhoff's theorem
concepts.definition: Any spherically symmetric solution of the vacuum Einstein equations (asymptotically flat, in the book's statement) is the Schwarzschild metric, even without assuming it is static; hence the exterior of a spherical body is static with constant mass however the body moves radially.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited from Misner, Thorne and Wheeler as a generalization of the static derivation, starting from Eq. 10.5; used later to argue that a collapsing star keeps a Schwarzschild exterior.

concepts.name: absence of monopole gravitational radiation
aliases: no gravitational waves from spherical pulsation
concepts.definition: A spherically symmetric system, even if it pulsates or collapses, cannot emit gravitational waves, because its exterior is fixed by Birkhoff's theorem; the analogue is the absence of monopole electromagnetic radiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn as a corollary of Birkhoff's theorem and tied to the linearized-theory result of Exercise 9.47.

concepts.name: Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equation
concepts.definition: The equation of hydrostatic equilibrium for a static, spherically symmetric perfect-fluid star in general relativity: dp/dr = -(rho + p)(m + 4 pi r^3 p)/[r(r - 2m)], to be solved with dm/dr = 4 pi r^2 rho and an equation of state.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by dividing the conservation equation by rho + p and eliminating Phi' with the (r,r) Einstein equation; then dissected in its Newtonian limit and solved exactly for uniform density.
concepts.notes: The book spells the third name Volkov; the 1939 paper is usually cited as Volkoff.

concepts.name: regularity at the centre
concepts.definition: If the spacetime contains a centre r = 0, local flatness there requires the ratio of circumference to proper radius of small circles to be 2 pi, so g_rr(0) = 1 and m(r)/r -> 0 as r -> 0 (m vanishing faster than r).
concepts.how_introduced: Argued from the circumference-to-radius ratio 2 pi |g_rr|^{-1/2} of a tiny circle; flagged as the first time the chapter assumes the centre belongs to the spacetime.

concepts.name: one-parameter family of stellar models
aliases: stellar sequence parametrized by central density
concepts.definition: For a given barotropic equation of state, static spherical stars are uniquely determined by their central pressure or density, because the two first-order structure equations need two initial values and one (m(0) = 0) is fixed by regularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a consequence of ODE uniqueness theorems; later realized concretely by the beta sequence of Buchdahl models and the numerical sequence of Exercise 10.17.

concepts.name: stellar surface and matching conditions
aliases: continuity of metric at the surface
concepts.definition: The star's surface R is where the pressure falls to zero (pressure must be continuous to avoid infinite forces, and vanishes in vacuum); there the interior metric functions are joined continuously to the Schwarzschild exterior, which fixes M = m(R) and the boundary value e^{2Phi(R)} = 1 - 2M/R.
concepts.how_introduced: Laid out as an integration recipe in §10.5 and executed for both exact solutions; the bibliography cautions that full junction conditions are more demanding.

concepts.name: junction conditions
aliases: matching across a surface of discontinuity
concepts.definition: The rules for joining two solutions of Einstein's equations across a hypersurface, requiring continuity of the induced metric and (absent a surface layer) of the extrinsic curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned only in the bibliography as the rigorous version of the chapter's continuity requirement on g_00 and g_rr, with references to MTW and Wald.

concepts.name: gravitational binding energy in the total mass
concepts.definition: The total mass M = integral of 4 pi r^2 rho dr is taken over coordinate volume, whereas proper volume is e^Lambda 4 pi r^2 dr, so M is not the sum of the fluid's locally measured energies; the difference encodes (negative) gravitational binding energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as a warning immediately after the Newtonian-looking formula (10.41), to show the care needed when importing Newtonian interpretations.
concepts.notes: The printed text says the angular integral gives 4 pi r^2 e^{Phi+Lambda} dr; from Eq. 10.42 it should be 4 pi r^2 e^Lambda dr (see gaps).

concepts.name: compactness bound 2m < r in static stars
aliases: no horizon inside a static star
concepts.definition: Throughout the interior of a static fluid star, 2m(r) < r: if r - 2m approached zero the TOV pressure gradient would become arbitrarily steep and negative, driving p to zero (the surface) first, after which m is constant while r grows.
concepts.how_introduced: Proved by a short contradiction argument using the 1/epsilon behaviour of TOV; ensures g_rr stays finite and positive, consistent with the exponential parametrization.

concepts.name: Newtonian limit of the TOV equation
concepts.definition: When p << rho, 4 pi r^3 p << m and m << r, the TOV equation reduces to the Newtonian hydrostatic equation dp/dr = -rho m/r^2, with rho the mass density.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken before exact solutions to anchor intuition, citing Chandrasekhar's stellar-structure monograph; the comparison motivates the claim that relativity makes gravity effectively stronger.

concepts.name: pressure as a source of gravity
aliases: relativistic steepening of the pressure gradient
concepts.definition: In general relativity pressure contributes to both inertia (rho + p) and gravitating mass (m + 4 pi r^3 p), and the factor r - 2m further strengthens the effective pull, so a static relativistic star needs a steeper pressure gradient than its Newtonian counterpart; increasing pressure to resist gravity can therefore make gravity stronger, feeding collapse.
concepts.how_introduced: Observed by comparing each factor of Eq. 10.39 with Eq. 10.44 and loosely interpreted as a stronger field, with gravitational collapse as the extreme case.
prerequisites: Newtonian limit of the TOV equation
concepts.notes: The self-defeating nature of pressure support is implicit in the text rather than spelled out; tutors should make it explicit.

concepts.name: exact solution
concepts.definition: A solution of Einstein's equations that can be written down in closed form using elementary functions of the coordinates, rather than being known only through numerical integration or approximation.
concepts.how_introduced: Footnote 2 treats discovering such solutions as a craft that depends on a lucky choice of coordinates and geometry as much as on method, pointing to Stephani et al. for a catalogue; footnote 1 adds that if the equation of state is left free one can manufacture solutions by picking m(r), at the cost of an implied p(rho) that is usually unphysical.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild interior solution
concepts.definition: The exact static star of constant energy density rho: m = 4 pi rho r^3/3, p(r) = rho [sqrt(1 - 2Mr^2/R^3) - sqrt(1 - 2M/R)]/[3 sqrt(1 - 2M/R) - sqrt(1 - 2Mr^2/R^3)] and e^Phi = (3/2) sqrt(1 - 2M/R) - (1/2) sqrt(1 - 2Mr^2/R^3), whose central pressure diverges as M/R -> 4/9.
concepts.how_introduced: Chosen for solvability and pedagogic value despite implying infinite sound speed; motivated weakly by the near-uniform density of neutron-star interiors.

concepts.name: speed of sound and causality in stellar matter
concepts.definition: The adiabatic sound speed is (dp/drho)^{1/2}; a physically acceptable equation of state must keep it below the speed of light, which bounds how stiff matter can be and hence limits allowed stellar models.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to criticize the uniform-density model (infinite sound speed) and to bound Buchdahl's equation of state (p < p_*, rho < 7 p_*) and his compactness parameter.

concepts.name: Buchdahl interior solution
concepts.definition: An exact static perfect-fluid star with equation of state rho = 12 sqrt(p_* p) - 5p, expressed through an auxiliary radius r' and u = beta sin(Ar')/(Ar'); beta equals the surface compactness M/R, p_* sets only the scale, and causality restricts 0 < beta < 1/6.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted without derivation as a physically more reasonable exact solution that reduces to the n = 1 polytrope in the Newtonian limit; used to exhibit a whole sequence of models from Newtonian to strongly relativistic.
prerequisites: speed of sound and causality in stellar matter
concepts.notes: Footnote 3: Buchdahl's own notation for the parameters differs.

concepts.name: polytrope
concepts.definition: A Newtonian stellar model with equation of state p = K rho^{1 + 1/n}; the n = 1 case has the analytic density profile rho proportional to sin(Ar)/(Ar), and the ultrarelativistic white-dwarf law p = k rho^{4/3} is the n = 3 case.
concepts.how_introduced: Named when Buchdahl's equation of state reduces at small p to rho = 12 sqrt(p_* p); worked out in Exercise 10.14.
prerequisites: Newtonian limit of the TOV equation
concepts.notes: The book does not name p = k rho^{4/3} as the n = 3 polytrope; that identification is ours.

concepts.name: surface redshift
concepts.definition: The redshift of light emitted at a stellar surface and received at infinity, z_s = (1 - 2M/R)^{-1/2} - 1, a direct observable of compactness.
concepts.how_introduced: Follows from Eq. 10.13 once e^{2Phi(R)} = 1 - 2M/R; evaluated for the Buchdahl family (up to 0.22) and in Exercise 10.10 for Sun-like and neutron-star parameters.
prerequisites: gravitational redshift in a static spacetime

concepts.name: Buchdahl limit M/R < 4/9
concepts.definition: No static, spherically symmetric perfect-fluid star (with density non-increasing outward, an assumption the book leaves implicit) can have radius smaller than 9M/4; configurations more compact would need infinite central pressure, so they must collapse.
concepts.how_introduced: First seen as the divergence of p_c in the uniform-density solution, then stated as a general theorem (Buchdahl 1959) in §10.7 and used to argue that pushing a limiting star inward leads to a black hole.

concepts.name: gravitational collapse
concepts.definition: The runaway inward motion of a self-gravitating body when no pressure can sustain equilibrium; for a spherical star the exterior remains Schwarzschild throughout, and complete collapse produces a black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Foreshadowed by the steepening of the TOV gradient, then introduced through Buchdahl's theorem and developed astrophysically as core collapse of massive stars.
prerequisites: pressure as a source of gravity

concepts.name: main sequence
concepts.definition: The narrow band occupied by stably hydrogen-burning stars in a plot of surface temperature against luminosity; a star's position on it is set mainly by its mass, more massive stars being hotter, brighter and much shorter-lived.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as background for how stars evolve towards compact endpoints.

concepts.name: negative specific heat of self-gravitating systems
concepts.definition: A bound self-gravitating system that loses energy contracts and heats up, so its effective heat capacity is negative; this makes such systems thermodynamically unstable and drives core contraction after fuel exhaustion.
concepts.how_introduced: Pointed out when explaining why a star's core shrinks and heats once hydrogen is exhausted.
concepts.notes: The virial-theorem reasoning behind the claim is not given in the text.

concepts.name: red giant
concepts.definition: An evolved star with a hot helium-burning core and a hugely expanded, cooler envelope, very luminous but with a low surface temperature; strong winds strip its outer layers.
concepts.how_introduced: Described as the consequence of temperature-sensitive helium ignition forcing the envelope to expand into a core-halo structure.

concepts.name: white dwarf
concepts.definition: A compact stellar remnant, typically up to about a solar mass and roughly Earth-sized, composed of helium, carbon and oxygen nuclei and supported against gravity by the degeneracy pressure of its electrons; it has no nuclear energy source and slowly cools.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in the evolutionary narrative as the fate of stars below about 8 solar masses, then modelled as a relativistic degenerate electron gas carrying nuclear mass.

concepts.name: Chandrasekhar limit
concepts.definition: The maximum mass that electron degeneracy pressure can support against gravity, a mass fixed by fundamental constants, the proton mass and the nucleon-to-electron ratio mu; the order-of-magnitude estimate gives about 0.3 solar masses and full integration about 1.3-1.4 solar masses for mu = 2.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed historically (Chandrasekhar 1930, Nobel 1983), then derived by scaling the Newtonian structure equations with p = k rho^{4/3} and noticing R cancels.
prerequisites: ultrarelativistic equation of state p = rho/3
concepts.notes: The book quotes 1.3 solar masses; the standard modern value for mu_e = 2 is about 1.44. See gaps for an inconsistent prefactor in Eq. 10.85.

concepts.name: core-collapse supernova
concepts.definition: The explosion that follows the collapse of the iron core of a massive star to a proto-neutron star; neutrinos from neutronization can reverse the infall of the envelope and eject it, leaving a neutron star, while failed or fallback-dominated explosions leave a black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Told as the climax of massive-star evolution, then refined with mass ranges, metallicity dependence, nucleosynthesis and hypernovae.

concepts.name: Pauli exclusion principle and phase-space cells
aliases: counting quantum states in momentum space
concepts.definition: Because momentum cannot be specified more finely than Delta p ~ h V^{-1/3}, momentum space is divided into cells of volume h^3/V, each holding at most two spin-1/2 fermions; this caps the number of particles with momenta in a shell and forces a cold Fermi gas to occupy high-momentum states.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from the uncertainty principle heuristically, then combined with spin degeneracy to count available states (Eqs. 10.71-10.73).

concepts.name: Fermi momentum
concepts.definition: The largest momentum occupied when N fermions fill the lowest states in volume V; with two spin states per cell n = 8 pi p_f^3/(3h^3), so p_f depends only on number density, not on particle mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by filling momentum states from zero upward in the coldest configuration.
prerequisites: Pauli exclusion principle and phase-space cells

concepts.name: degenerate Fermi gas
concepts.definition: A gas of fermions so dense or cold that all momentum states up to the Fermi momentum are filled; its energy density and pressure are fixed by density alone and remain large even at zero temperature.
concepts.how_introduced: Constructed by 'cooling as far as possible' and integrating single-particle energies sqrt(p^2 + m^2) over the Fermi sphere.

concepts.name: degeneracy pressure
concepts.definition: The pressure of a degenerate Fermi gas arising from the exclusion principle rather than thermal motion; it supports white dwarfs (electrons) and neutron stars (neutrons).
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from p = -dE/dV at fixed particle number using the first law with no heat flow, yielding Eq. 10.77.

concepts.name: ultrarelativistic equation of state p = rho/3
concepts.definition: For particles whose momenta far exceed their rest mass, energy density scales as p_f^4 and pressure equals one third of energy density, exactly as for a photon gas, since rest mass becomes negligible.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived as the p_f >> m limit of the degenerate gas and linked to the photon-gas result of Exercise 4.22; used for neutron-star matter and in Exercises 10.16-10.17.
concepts.notes: Exercise 10.16: because p = rho/3 contains no dimensional constant, its only self-similar stellar solution is singular (rho = 3/(56 pi r^2), m = 3r/14).

concepts.name: order-of-magnitude stellar structure
concepts.definition: Replacing derivatives in the stellar-structure equations by ratios over the radius (dm/dr -> M/R, dp/dr -> p/R) and dropping numerical factors to obtain scaling relations among mass, radius, typical density and pressure.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to extract the Chandrasekhar mass from p = k rho^{4/3} in a few lines.
prerequisites: Newtonian limit of the TOV equation

concepts.name: neutronization instability
concepts.definition: Once the density is high enough (the book says above about 10^10 kg/m^3) electrons become energetic enough to combine with protons into neutrons, emitting neutrinos; removing electrons from the pressure-supporting gas makes pressure grow too slowly with density, so matter between white-dwarf and neutron-star densities is unstable to collapse.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to explain the slightly lower actual white-dwarf mass limit and the absence of stable stars at intermediate central densities.
concepts.notes: The book's threshold is low; composition-dependent estimates are about 1e12-1e14 kg/m^3 (see gaps).

concepts.name: neutron star
concepts.definition: A compact remnant of about 1-2 solar masses and radius about 10-12 km, with central density near or above nuclear density (about 10^17 kg/m^3), made mostly of degenerate neutrons (with superfluid and possibly quark phases) and supported by neutron degeneracy pressure and nuclear forces; M/R is about 0.15, making it strongly relativistic.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached as the only stable state after neutronization; contrasted with white dwarfs (heavier fermion, no separate mass gas) and then characterized by estimates, history and observations.

concepts.name: pulsar
concepts.definition: A rotating, strongly magnetized neutron star whose magnetic axis is misaligned with its spin axis, so beamed radiation from its polar regions sweeps past the observer once per rotation, producing periodic pulses from radio to gamma rays.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced through the 1967 discovery by Bell and Hewish, with spin-frequency range, field strengths, emission modelling (Philippov et al. 2019) and use as mass probes in binaries.

concepts.name: break-up spin frequency
concepts.definition: The maximum rotation rate of a star, reached when the equatorial speed equals the orbital speed sqrt(M/R) just above the surface; for a neutron star of M/R ~ 0.15 and R = 10 km it corresponds to about 1.8 kHz.
concepts.how_introduced: Estimated in Newtonian terms to show how fast neutron stars can spin, compared with the 716 Hz record pulsar.

concepts.name: gravitational binding energy release in collapse
concepts.definition: Forming a compact star releases a large fraction of the rest-mass energy of its constituents, because a particle at rest on the surface has energy at infinity m sqrt(1 - 2M/R), far below m for compact stars; this exceeds nuclear-fusion efficiencies of 0.1-1%.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated with a forward reference to Chapter 11's energy formula, and used by Baade and Zwicky to argue neutron-star formation could power supernovae.
concepts.notes: The printed formula reads m sqrt(1 - M/R) and the quoted 8% follows from it; with the correct factor 1 - 2M/R and M/R = 0.15 the fraction is about 16% (our estimate).

concepts.name: neutron-star equation of state and maximum mass
concepts.definition: Uncertainty in the behaviour of matter above nuclear density yields many candidate equations of state with different mass-radius relations and maximum masses, up to about 2.5 solar masses; the maximum is generally believed to be below 3 solar masses, beyond which collapse to a black hole is unavoidable.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the lack of a simple argument for a neutron-star mass limit with p = rho/3, then linked to pulsar mass measurements (about 1.4, and 2.14 for PSR J0740+6620) and gravitational-wave constraints.

concepts.name: pulsar kicks
concepts.definition: The high space velocities (typically 400-1000 km/s) that neutron stars acquire at birth from asymmetries in collapse and explosion; kicks, together with sudden mass loss, usually unbind binaries but can occasionally keep them bound.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented through pulsar proper-motion studies and used to explain why double neutron-star binaries are rare.

concepts.name: metallicity and opacity
concepts.definition: Metallicity is the relative abundance of elements heavier than helium; such elements raise the opacity of stellar gas, which traps radiation, affects how much envelope a supernova ejects, and limits the mass of stars that can form.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the deciding factor for the fate of stars above about 25 solar masses and for the masses of stars forming in pristine gas.

concepts.name: stellar-mass black hole
concepts.definition: A black hole formed from the collapse of a massive star, with mass from about 5 to about 60 solar masses depending on the progenitor.
concepts.how_introduced: Described as the outcome when fallback onto the neutron-star core forces further collapse; forward pointer to Chapter 11.

concepts.name: compact-object mass gaps
concepts.definition: Ranges of mass expected to be sparsely populated by stellar remnants: a lower gap between the maximum neutron-star mass (below 3 solar masses) and the lightest supernova black holes (about 5 solar masses), and an upper gap near 60-150 solar masses where massive stars are disrupted entirely by an instability instead of leaving black holes.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a consequence of the neutron-star maximum mass and supernova physics, then linked to gravitational-wave events GW190814 and GW190521 that seem to populate the gaps.
prerequisites: neutron-star equation of state and maximum mass
concepts.notes: The text does not name the instability; it is usually called the pair instability.

concepts.name: intermediate-mass black hole
concepts.definition: A black hole with mass between stellar-mass and supermassive, roughly hundreds to thousands of solar masses, possibly left by very massive zero-metallicity first-generation stars.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned while discussing the first stars and the upper mass gap; supermassive black holes deferred to Chapter 11.

concepts.name: hypernova
concepts.definition: An exceptionally energetic core-collapse explosion expected for the most massive progenitors (initial masses well above roughly 40 solar masses in the book's account), accompanied by a long-duration gamma-ray burst and typically associated with black-hole formation.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in passing (italicized) at the top end of the mass-to-remnant map in the supernova subsection, and pointed to again in the bibliography's supernova reading list.

key_equations.name: Minkowski metric in spherical coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Flat spacetime written in spherical polar coordinates; the starting template for spherical symmetry.

key_equations.name: Two-sphere line element
key_equations.meaning: Metric on a sphere of constant t and r; defines dOmega^2. Area 4 pi r^2 and circumference 2 pi r are read from the coefficient.

key_equations.name: Symmetry spheres in curved spacetime
key_equations.meaning: Precise statement of spherical symmetry: each event lies on a sphere whose area 4 pi f depends only on the remaining two coordinates; r is then defined by f = r^2.
key_equations.symbols: f: unknown area function; r', t: the other two coordinates

key_equations.name: Metric after radial orthogonality
key_equations.meaning: Intermediate form after requiring radial lines to be orthogonal to the spheres (g_r theta = g_r phi = 0).

key_equations.name: General spherically symmetric metric
key_equations.meaning: Most general spherically symmetric metric in adapted coordinates, with g_00, g_0r, g_rr functions of t and r; starting point for Birkhoff's theorem.

key_equations.name: Time-reversal transformation of metric components
key_equations.latex: g_{\bar0\bar0}=(\Lambda^0{}_{\bar0})^2g_{00}=g_{00},\quad g_{\bar0\bar r}=\Lambda^0{}_{\bar0}\Lambda^r{}_{\bar r}g_{0r}=-g_{0r},\quad g_{\bar r\bar r}=g_{rr}
key_equations.meaning: Under t -> -t only the dt dr cross term flips sign, so invariance of a static geometry forces g_0r = 0.

key_equations.name: Static spherically symmetric metric
key_equations.meaning: General static spherical metric with two unknown radial functions; valid while g_00 < 0 and g_rr > 0.

key_equations.name: Asymptotic flatness conditions
key_equations.meaning: Boundary conditions for an isolated star: spacetime becomes flat far away.

key_equations.name: Proper radial distance
key_equations.meaning: Physical length of a radial path at fixed t and angles; shows r is not distance.

key_equations.name: Energy at infinity
key_equations.meaning: Conserved covariant time component of four-momentum along geodesics of a t-independent metric, named minus the energy at infinity.

key_equations.name: Locally measured energy
key_equations.meaning: Energy measured by a static observer at radius r, with U^0 = e^{-Phi}; exceeds E deep in the potential.

key_equations.name: Redshift definition
key_equations.meaning: Standard definition of redshift in terms of wavelengths or frequencies.

key_equations.name: Gravitational redshift from a static field
key_equations.meaning: Redshift of a photon emitted by a static source at r_1 and received at infinity; gives e^Phi observational meaning.

key_equations.name: Einstein tensor G_00
key_equations.meaning: Time-time Einstein tensor component of the static metric; depends only on Lambda, which is why m(r) is natural.

key_equations.name: Einstein tensor G_rr
key_equations.meaning: Radial Einstein tensor component; the only one containing Phi' at first order.

key_equations.name: Einstein tensor G_theta theta
key_equations.meaning: Angular Einstein tensor component; its field equation is redundant by the Bianchi identity.
Spherical symmetry relates the two angular components.
Normalization of the fluid four-velocity.

key_equations.name: Static fluid four-velocity
key_equations.meaning: Only nonzero components of a fluid at rest in static coordinates.

key_equations.name: Static perfect-fluid stress-energy
key_equations.meaning: Nonzero covariant components of the perfect-fluid stress-energy tensor for a static star.
key_equations.symbols: rho: total energy density; p: pressure

key_equations.name: General equation of state
key_equations.meaning: Pressure as a function of energy density and specific entropy for a fluid in local thermodynamic equilibrium.

key_equations.name: Barotropic equation of state
key_equations.meaning: Equation of state when entropy is constant or negligible; closes the stellar-structure system.

key_equations.name: Conservation of stress-energy
key_equations.meaning: Local energy-momentum conservation; only the alpha = r component is nontrivial for a static spherical star.

key_equations.name: Relativistic hydrostatic equilibrium
key_equations.meaning: Pressure gradient required to hold static fluid against gravity; inertia is rho + p.

key_equations.name: Mass function definition
key_equations.meaning: Replacement for Lambda chosen to make the (0,0) equation Newtonian in form.
Radial metric component in terms of the mass function.

key_equations.name: Mass equation
key_equations.meaning: The (0,0) Einstein equation: identical in form to Newtonian mass accumulation, integrated over coordinate (not proper) volume.

key_equations.name: Potential gradient equation
key_equations.meaning: The (r,r) Einstein equation: gravity's pull is sourced by m plus a pressure term and enhanced by 1/(r - 2m).

key_equations.name: Vacuum structure equations
key_equations.meaning: Structure equations outside the star where rho = p = 0.

key_equations.name: Exterior solution
key_equations.meaning: Integration of the vacuum equations with Phi -> 0 at infinity.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild metric
key_equations.meaning: Unique vacuum exterior of any spherically symmetric body of mass M.

key_equations.name: Large-r Schwarzschild
key_equations.meaning: First-order expansion far from the source.

key_equations.name: Far-field metric in quasi-Cartesian coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Matches the weak-field metric of a Newtonian mass M (Eq. 8.60), identifying M as the physical mass.
key_equations.symbols: R here is the isotropic radius, not the stellar radius

key_equations.name: Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equation
key_equations.meaning: General-relativistic hydrostatic equilibrium; with dm/dr and an EOS it determines the star.

key_equations.name: Mass matching
key_equations.meaning: Continuity of g_rr at the surface identifies the exterior mass with the mass function at the surface.

key_equations.name: Total mass integral
key_equations.meaning: Looks Newtonian but integrates over coordinate volume; binding energy is hidden in the difference from proper volume.

key_equations.name: Proper volume element
key_equations.meaning: Proper volume in a t = const slice (spatial metric determinant). After angular integration this is 4 pi r^2 e^Lambda dr; the printed e^{Phi+Lambda} in the following sentence is inconsistent.

key_equations.name: Surface boundary value of g_00
key_equations.meaning: Continuity of g_00 supplies the integration constant for Phi inside.

key_equations.name: Newtonian hydrostatic equilibrium
key_equations.meaning: Limit of TOV for p << rho, m << r; all relativistic factors steepen the gradient relative to this.

key_equations.name: Uniform density assumption
key_equations.meaning: Replaces the equation of state and integrates the mass equation immediately.
Mass function outside the uniform star equals the Schwarzschild mass.

key_equations.name: TOV for uniform density
key_equations.meaning: Separable form of TOV when rho is constant.

key_equations.name: Integrated uniform-density pressure relation
key_equations.meaning: Implicit pressure profile from central pressure p_c.

key_equations.name: Radius from central pressure
key_equations.meaning: Surface condition p(R) = 0 applied to Eq. 10.49.

key_equations.name: Central pressure of a uniform-density star
key_equations.meaning: Diverges when M/R -> 4/9.

key_equations.name: Uniform-density pressure profile
key_equations.meaning: Explicit pressure inside the Schwarzschild interior solution.

key_equations.name: Uniform-density potential
key_equations.meaning: Lapse function inside the uniform star, fixed by g_00(R) = -(1 - 2M/R); gives central redshift.

key_equations.name: Buchdahl equation of state
key_equations.meaning: Equation of state for Buchdahl's exact solution; causal for suitable parameters.
key_equations.symbols: p_*: arbitrary constant setting the scale

key_equations.name: Low-pressure limit of Buchdahl EOS
key_equations.meaning: An n = 1 polytrope (p proportional to rho^2).

key_equations.name: Causality bounds for Buchdahl EOS
key_equations.meaning: Requirement that dp/drho < 1 everywhere.

key_equations.name: Buchdahl auxiliary radial coordinate
key_equations.meaning: Defines the coordinate r' in which the solution is simple.
key_equations.symbols: beta: second constant, equal to M/R

key_equations.name: Buchdahl metric functions
key_equations.meaning: Metric of Buchdahl's star for Ar' <= pi.

key_equations.name: Buchdahl pressure and density
key_equations.meaning: Matter profiles of the Buchdahl solution.

key_equations.name: Buchdahl surface values
key_equations.meaning: At u = 0 (Ar' = pi) the solution matches Schwarzschild with M/R = beta.

key_equations.name: Surface redshift
key_equations.meaning: Redshift from the stellar surface in terms of compactness beta = M/R.

key_equations.name: Buchdahl mass
key_equations.meaning: Total mass of the Buchdahl star; p_* sets the scale only.

key_equations.name: Buchdahl pressure-to-density ratio
key_equations.meaning: Largest at the centre; used with causality.

key_equations.name: Causal range of Buchdahl compactness
key_equations.meaning: Causality (p_c/rho_c < 1/7) limits Buchdahl stars to M/R < 1/6, surface redshift below 0.22.

key_equations.name: Buchdahl's theorem
key_equations.meaning: No static spherical star can be more compact than R = 9M/4; stated in words in §10.7 (Buchdahl 1959).

key_equations.name: Momentum uncertainty in a box
key_equations.meaning: Heuristic minimum momentum resolution for a particle confined to volume V.

key_equations.name: Counting momentum states
key_equations.latex: dN=\frac{4\pi p^2dp}{(\Delta p)^3}=\frac{4\pi p^2dp}{h^3}V,\qquad N_{max}=V\frac{8\pi p^2dp}{h^3}
key_equations.meaning: Number of momentum cells in a shell, doubled for spin: the maximum number of fermions with those momenta.

key_equations.name: Fermi momentum
key_equations.meaning: Filling all states up to p_f; p_f depends only on number density.
key_equations.symbols: p_f: Fermi momentum; n: number density

key_equations.name: Energy density of a degenerate gas
key_equations.meaning: Total energy per volume of a cold Fermi gas.

key_equations.name: Pressure from the first law (intermediate)
key_equations.meaning: Adiabatic compression at fixed N. The book prints V dp_f/dV = -n dp_f/dn = +p_f/3; the correct value is -p_f/3, which is what yields the final result.

key_equations.name: Degenerate gas pressure
key_equations.meaning: Exact zero-temperature pressure of a Fermi gas.

key_equations.name: Ultrarelativistic degenerate gas
key_equations.meaning: For p_f >> m the gas behaves like radiation.

key_equations.name: White-dwarf mass density
key_equations.meaning: Gravitating density comes from nuclei; mu is nucleons per electron.
key_equations.symbols: mu ~ 1-2; m_p proton mass; n_e electron number density

key_equations.name: Relativistic white-dwarf equation of state
key_equations.meaning: Pressure from ultrarelativistic electrons, density from nuclei.

key_equations.name: Newtonian structure equations
key_equations.meaning: Adequate for white dwarfs.

key_equations.name: Order-of-magnitude structure
key_equations.meaning: Scaling version of the structure equations with the 4/3 law inserted.

key_equations.name: Chandrasekhar mass estimate
key_equations.meaning: Radius cancels, leaving a unique mass. Printed inconsistency: with Eq. 10.81 the right-hand expression equals k^{3/2} (what Eq. 10.83 gives), while the middle expression is (3/4 pi)^{1/2} ~ 0.49 times that; the quoted number 0.47 x 10^5 cm matches k^{3/2}.

key_equations.name: Numerical Chandrasekhar estimate
key_equations.meaning: Order-of-magnitude white-dwarf maximum mass; precise value about 1.3 solar masses.

key_equations.name: Neutron-star matter equation of state
key_equations.meaning: Neutrons provide both pressure and energy density at high compression.

key_equations.name: Break-up velocity
key_equations.meaning: Equatorial orbital speed; gives maximum spin 1.8 kHz for R = 10 km.

key_equations.name: Energy at infinity of a particle at rest on the surface
key_equations.meaning: Gives the fraction of rest mass released in forming a compact star. The book prints m sqrt(1 - M/R) (and 8%), which is a misprint of this Chapter 11 result.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild in isotropic coordinates
key_equations.latex: ds^2=-\left(\frac{1-M/2\bar r}{1+M/2\bar r}\right)^2dt^2+\left(1+\frac{M}{2\bar r}\right)^4(d\bar r^2+\bar r^2d\Omega^2),\quad r=\bar r(1+M/2\bar r)^2
key_equations.meaning: Exercise 10.9 result; proves Eq. 10.38 at large r-bar.

key_equations.name: Lane-Emden equation for n = 1
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian n = 1 polytrope, the limit of Buchdahl's solution (Exercise 10.14).

key_equations.name: Stiff piecewise neutron-star EOS
key_equations.meaning: Crude realistic EOS for the numerical model sequence of Exercise 10.17.

figures.label: Figure 10.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two flat sheets joined by a narrow circular throat: the surface is symmetric about an axis, yet the axis (the would-be centre of every circle) is not part of the surface.
figures.visual_description: Line drawing in perspective of two horizontal parallelogram-shaped planes, one above the other. A slender vertical tube (throat) connects them, flaring into each plane like a trumpet bell. Around the throat on each sheet are concentric ellipses (circles seen in perspective), and short curved lines radiate outward from the throat across both sheets like spokes. Dashed lines mark hidden parts of the throat's rim. No labels, axes or arrows.
figures.what_it_teaches: Symmetry orbits (circles, or spheres in 3D) can carry an areal radius r defined purely by their circumference or area even when the space contains no central point; r therefore need not be a distance from a centre, and the minimum r at the throat is not zero.

redesign.idea: A 3D surface of revolution the learner reshapes: a plane with a smooth bump, a cone-like funnel, or a two-sheeted throat. Circles of symmetry are drawn on it; for any circle the app shows its circumference-derived areal radius r = C/(2 pi) next to the proper distance measured along the surface from the axis (or from the throat), revealing when they agree, when they differ, and when no centre exists.
redesign.interaction: Slider morphs the profile function z(r) from flat to curved to throat (continuously pinching the centre out of the surface); drag a ring up and down the surface; toggle a readout of C/(2 pi), proper radial distance and the ratio C/(proper radius), which must tend to 2 pi at a regular centre.

worked_examples.label: Reducing the spherically symmetric metric (in-text derivation)
worked_examples.problem: Find the most general form of the metric compatible with spherical symmetry.
worked_examples.method: Label spheres by areal radius r; demand radial coordinate lines be orthogonal to the spheres (kills g_r theta, g_r phi); argue that nonzero g_t theta, g_t phi would define a tangent vector field on each sphere, which symmetry forbids.
worked_examples.key_insight: Symmetry requirements are imposed as orthogonality conditions on basis vectors, i.e. as vanishing metric components.
